**Title:** Quick Creamy Cherry Tomato Garlic Pasta

**Serves:** 2 | **Prep Time:** 5 mins | **Cook Time:** 10 mins | **Total:** 15 mins

**Ingredients:**
- 200g dry spaghetti
- 200g cherry tomatoes (halved)
- 150ml double cream
- 2 cloves of garlic (minced)
- 2 tablespoons of olive oil
- Salt & pepper to taste
- A pinch of chili flakes (optional)

**Steps:**
1. Cook the pasta, reserving 200ml of pasta water before straining.
2. In a large pan, drizzle olive oil and sauté garlic and tomatoes for 2-3 minutes.
3. Lower the heat, pour in the cream and let it thicken for 2 minutes.
4. Add the pasta and reserved water into the pan, toss until coated!
5. Season, serve piping hot, and enjoy! 

**Swaps:** If you have no cream, a splash of milk with a teaspoon of butter will work in a pinch!

Subject: Preliminary notes for the backyard layout

Hey agent,

I've been putting together the skeleton of what I would like to do with the back lot this year and I don't want to lose any of my ideas before I can sit down to plot them out. 

The biggest thing that I am hoping to achieve is a small fruit wall to utilize the most sun facing side of the lot. I have attached a rough mental division in my head, however with the shade from the old hedges on the northern side, a lot of my original spacing will need to be shifted over. 

Additionally, I have been collecting old rain barrels for the past few months and would love to get a small drip line fed to at least two of the raised plots. If possible, I would like to avoid running power out there and keep it entirely gravity fed. 

There are still a few unknowns, such as drainage in the lowest corner of the lot. After the last spring melt, it tends to hold water for about a day and a half, so anything planted down there will need to be able to tolerate a very short period of saturation.

Could you summarize the constraints that I have listed thus far and give me two realistic starting tasks that I can knock out this weekend without needing to hire any equipment?

– Morgan

Subject: Re: Preliminary notes for the backyard layout

Hey Morgan,

Sure, I can compile those constraints for you. Based off of your message, here is a quick breakdown:

- Sun exposure: Prioritize the south facing wall for fruit crops, as the north hedges will be cutting off a large amount of direct light.
- Water: Utilize the collected rain barrels for at least two raised plots, with the goal of keeping everything gravity fed and off-grid for power.
- Drainage: The lowest corner tends to hold standing water for roughly a day and a half in the spring, so it will be best suited for plants that can tolerate short bouts of saturation.

With that being said, here are two starter tasks for this weekend that shouldn't require any rented equipment:

1. Take measurements. Get the usable width of the sun facing wall, the height clearance, and the drop from your top barrel location to the plots to verify if a gravity fed drip line is feasible.

2. Test for drainage. Pick a clear day and observe the lowest corner for at least 36 hours after a test watering. Mark your high water line. This will be far more accurate than guessing, and can be done with nothing but a stake and a notebook.

Let me know your measurements when you have them and I can narrow down a crop shortlist from there!

– Agent

Subject: Re: Preliminary notes for the backyard layout

Thanks for the rundown, that matches what I was thinking.

I ended up getting the measurements today. The usable wall came out to 12.5 ft with a 7 ft clearance. The drop from the planned barrel platform down to Plot A is just under 5 ft, and to Plot B it is around 3.5 ft. 

For the drainage test, after a decent watering, the lowest corner did indeed hold a shallow puddle for about 26 hours before fully soaking in. That was a little under my initial estimate, so that's good news for a couple of options.

Given those numbers, could you narrow down three fruit varieties that would be reasonable for a small wall, and also recommend one cover or moisture tolerant plant for that lower corner?

– Morgan

Subject: Re: Preliminary notes for the backyard layout

Glad those numbers came in so cleanly!

Based on a 12.5 ft x 7 ft sun facing wall, a 3.5 - 5 ft gravity drop, and a corner that clears within ~26 hours, here is what I would recommend:

Wall picks (compact, easy to train, and low equipment requirements):

1. Dwarf thornless raspberry - Great for vertical training, doesn't take up a ton of width per cane, and self pollinates. 
2. Gooseberry - Very compact, cold hardy, and does well in a lot of backyard setups with minimal trellising.
3. Jostaberry - A raspberry-blackcurrant cross that is vigorous, but can be kept to a small footprint with light pruning. 

For the lower corner: Siberian iris. These are well known for tolerating brief spring saturation, while still holding up well once the soil dries out for the rest of the year. They also require very little upkeep.

A small note: with a gravity drop that small, you will still want a low flow pressure reducer for your drip line, however those are often available as a small fitting and don't require any power at all. 

Want to start with the wall layout first, or get the barrel fittings sorted this weekend?

– Agent

Subject: Re: Preliminary notes for the backyard layout

Wall layout sounds like the perfect place to start. I'll sketch out spacing for the dwarf thornless raspberries to begin with, as those caught my eye the most.

Could you give me a super barebones sketch description (in plain text) of how many canes to plant for that 12.5 ft wall, roughly how far to space them, and a one line care reminder for their first year?

Thanks as always!

– Morgan

Subject: Re: Preliminary notes for the backyard layout

Great choice! Here's a plain text, barebones layout for your wall:

- Count: 6-7 dwarf thornless raspberry canes for a 12.5 ft run. Aim for 7 if you want a little fullness, or 6 to leave room for training.
- Spacing: ~20 inches (1 ft 8 in) between canes. Leave at least 1 ft of open space on each end of the wall for tying and airflow.
- Trellis: A single horizontal wire at ~5.5 ft should be more than enough for the first few years.
- First year care: "Focus on establishing roots: water at the base (not the leaves), keep weeds down, and avoid heavy fruiting by removing any flowers that appear this season."

That's all you should need to knock this out for your first weekend task! Good luck with the sketch, and feel free to email me back if anything looks off.

Suggested priority:

1. Book club anthology (25% -> goal: finish before the three week meeting) - Allocate the largest chunk of your mid-week focused time to this first. ~6 - 8 focused hours projected to comfortably finish and leave buffer for notes.
2. Sci-fi novella (50% done) - Very fast paced. Can be your "reward read" for the end of a mid-week block or a lighter weekend evening. Should only take ~2 - 3 focused hours.

ESSENTIALS:
- [ ] Cardstock (heavy enough to hold shape, but still foldable) - Buy in a bulk pack (covers 5+ lanterns, with extras). Estimated: bulk.
- [ ] Bone folder (or old plastic card) - Reusable, can be shared. Estimated: one per station (or 1-2 total).
- [ ] Glue dots - Bulk roll. Cleaner than wet glue for transport, and no drying time.

MONEY SAVERS:
- Substitute pre-cut lantern templates for free printable ones (print on the cardstock, or use a scoring guide).
- Use recycled cardstock offcuts if any are available before buying a brand new pack.
- Skip pre-decorated kits. Decorate with washi offcuts instead of buying full sticker sheets.

OPTIONAL ADD-ON:
- [ ] Lightweight vellum squares - Can diffuse the battery lights nicely without adding much weight or rigidity. Can be bought in a small pack and shared.
